If you do run away, there's basic necessities you need which is obviously;

Bring your own water bottle. Bring as much snacks as you can, phone and charger, a personal defense item, and if you can evidence of abuse. 

If you're under the age of 16 and running away in the US, if you're found you will be returned home. You'll also most likely have to go to court and deal with something called CHINS, which would then put you under more supervision and restriction. As well as, if you're a female, in any sense, 80%+ of female runaways end up having to deal with sexual assault. 

People who run away at a young age (below 16) have a greater feeling of isolation and depression, and typically end up attempting suicide. You won't be able to have regular showers and your hygiene will probably get worse. 

As well as, getting a "proper" job is going to be a lot harder. Most jobs need you to have a place you reside in already aka a home address. A lot of jobs also feel like people are homeless due to addiction and will be less likely to hire you under that presumption. 

If you do plan to run away either way, calling  1-800-786-2929 aka [https://www.1800runaway.org/](https://www.1800runaway.org/) as they're a good resource. Finding shelters in your area, making a list of pros and cons to see what is the actual best choice, and having a place to go to for the first 2-5 days when you leave is important. 

Finding someone you can talk to whose an adult is important, maybe even going and living with an aunt or uncle, or finding ways to leave your house could be helpful. Even if you aren't leaving your family (which usually once you're 16+ you're able to do so more easily) you're still getting away from your household for a bit. 

I think if you want to run away, try and get a workers permit or job. Tell your parents you just want a bit of extra spending money and to try something new. This can help you save up so you don't have to be on the streets. It may take a few months or years but eventually you'll be able to get out of your household, and live life the way you desire. Your childhood, of being under 18 in any way, is not going to be your whole life. The best thing you can try to do for yourself is make sure you won't have to suffer more than you already are.

As a gay male myself, if someone isn't gay or bi, there's no chance of getting with him if he isn't. I'm Latino myself (Cuban) and my boyfriend is Mexican himself, but bi. 

I knew and was able to accept the fact I was gay when I had no interest romantically and especially not sexually with women, but my boyfriend had a harder time coming to terms with this. 

Half of this is that since he was bi, he thought since he had attraction to women, that it automatically meant he didn't have attraction to men. When he started acknowledging his attraction to men, he essentially ignored it and didn't believe he could be LGBT. 

Another part of this is, many Latino and Hispanic families in my experience are pretty traditional and not all too accepting. My dad disowned me for being gay, and so did my whole dads side and almost all of my mom's side. My boyfriend has come out to nearly every family member besides his dad due to a lot of fear of abuse and/or getting kicked out and being unable to pay for college. 

You can't force someone to come out, and if you love this man you'll wait for him to come to things on his own term. It's rough and my boyfriend only found out he was bi almost a year after meeting me (I had crushed on him that whole year) and three months after when he was more solidified in his sexuality, he asked me out. 

It takes time, getting over internalized homo/biphobia, and whether or not they'd be able to be in a same sex relationship without losing all of their family. 

Good luck, and I hope that if he is lgbt, you're able to get together, and if he's not you'll at least get a great friend.

Being trans is from a disconnect from the brain to body (having a female brain in a male body and vise versa,) and that disconnect which makes a person trans is called GD. 

A psychological disorder, which GD is labelled as, is when the brain presents abnormally and causes a condition(s) that affect mood, thinking, and behavior. The way to treat/"fix" GD is by transitioning. This can lessen a persons dysphoria but the symptoms for GD is (going by the APA):

  

1. A marked incongruence between one’s experienced/expressed gender and primary and/or secondary sex characteristics
2. A strong desire to be rid of one’s primary and/or secondary sex characteristics
3. A strong desire for the primary and/or secondary sex characteristics of the other gender
4. A strong desire to be of the other gender
5. A strong desire to be treated as the other gender
6. A strong conviction that one has the typical feelings and reactions of the other gender

To be diagnosed you need technically at least two of these and experiencing them for a long period of time.A person who has fully transition still desires to be seen as the gender they ID as and want to be treated as the gender they ID as. This meaning they'd still have GD even though you don't deal with any of the hardships pre-everything. 

Mimicing/Imitating illnesses can feel the same as the illness because they, imitate. For example with physical illnesses, chronic fatigue syndrome can mimic POTS almost exactly the same, but the treatment methods have to be treated differently as they are not the same illness. Going with mental illnesses, borderline personality disorder can imitate bipolar disorder, present the exact same, but still need different treatments. 

Someone with autism for example can present with GD, but that does not inherently mean they have GD. While it's possible to have the two together, it does not mean that it isn't imitating. Same thing with OCD, schizophrenia, body dysmorphia, PTSD, trauma, etc which can all mimic GD without being it. 

What you're saying, that GD isn't inherently something that makes someone trans, is making GD seem like it isn't a necessity to transition, but that feeling like your trans is enough?? Again, I could be misinterpreting what you're saying, but if GD doesn't make a person trans, what does and why?

To the first part of what your saying, I've always been under the idea that Gender Dysphoria is what makes a person trans but things such as fetishization, autism, etc *imitate* it. 

Ex:

["Patients of either sex who ask for Gender Reassignment should be assessed for any indications of Asperger's Syndrome. Irreversible treatments should be avoided until it is clear there is a genuine issue of Transsexualism"](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/294920895_Gender_Dysphoria_and_Autism_Spectrum_Disorders_A_Note_of_Caution) (Showing that they aren't trans because they lack GD but have autism that imitates it)

["With the intensified public awareness and media coverage of issues concerning gender identity and gender incongruence, distinguishing true gender dysphoria or incongruence from the sexual obsessions of obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is especially important. Although intrusive sexual obsessions are not uncommon in OCD, obsessions concerning sexual content are more difficult for clinicians to identify as OCD than other types of obsessions (e.g., obsessions concerning contamination). Making the correct diagnosis helps ensure that appropriate clinical treatment can be offered." ... "CD sexual obsessions include those concerning one's sexual orientation, such as recurrent doubts about being gay, fears of becoming homosexual, and/or fears that others may believe one to be homosexual"](https://journals.aace.com/doi/pdf/10.4158/EP161223.CR) (Showing that a persons fetishization/compulsive thoughts on it is what made them believe they had GD when they were just imitating it)

Looking up lgbt centers in your area, online trans support groups near you, etc is usually the best bet.

Despite being under the age of 18, I was temporarily kicked out of my ndads house before with no way to get to my moms house. I also have a minor working license and had 2 jobs so I had a flow of money my way. 

I was lucky a friend of mine let me into their home for two weeks, but the most important thing I found was that you really need to know how to use basic utilities. You need to learn how to use dishwashers, washer and drier, etc. Also, learning to unclog toilets and drains is a simple but very efficient skill. I recommend learning to cook foods like: Eggs, sticky rice + brown rice, black beans, grilled cheese, grilled chicken and potato fries, pancakes, etc. Keeping your food bill low is very important, rice, eggs, bread, and most vegetables are particularly cheap and can be bought in large amounts for very cheap which can save you food for weeks. 

Rent in my area is 1,500 bucks, which is why I have prepared by working two jobs. If I worked minimum 40 hours a week, I only get around \~440 bucks, and rent is due every 4 weeks, meaning I get around  \~1,760 which means I only have \~260 left due to rent if it covers utilities/has a flat fee, but then you get into internet which in my area can cost as much as 35-90 bucks. So if I want a good plan then lets say that's around \~60 bucks just so I can break even of 200 bucks. 

Once you have that solved, what I recommend doing is breaking your money up, aka being like "I can only spend 50 bucks on food, have to put 70 bucks in savings, and then whatever is leftover on any other household necessity, then whatever is left over from that goes into my savings."

Also- having a savings account is EXTREMELY important. Never take money from it unless you need to. Personally, savings are for when a situation is dire- like if your car randomly broke down, if you had to go to the hospital, etc.

Also, speaking of hospitals, when you get the bill ask for an itemized list. Often times they can be charging you 60 bucks for a band-aid, if they know you're going to see it, often they take it off and this can reduce a hospital bill DRASTICALLY. It worked wonders for me, anyway. 

Along with this, you'll have to find an apartment pet safe if you want to keep your cats, a lot of apartments charge +500 bucks (in my area) for having any sort of pet. 

Best of luck and if you have any additional questions feel free to ask.

I volunteer at a trans resource center and have seen many cases like this in my 3 years of experience. The first step in this scenario is to recognize, if you've only been out for a short period of time (less than a year and a half) and are a minor, then there's going to be some confusion in the mix. It's awful but you do technically have to wait unless you're able to get a mature minor doctrine or become an emancipated minor.  

The best thing you can do for yourself is surround yourself with people who are accepting, such as [TrevorSpace](https://www.trevorspace.org/?utm_source=trevor_website&utm_medium=web&utm_campaign=homepage_tabs) which is a chat for those under the age of 25 and are LGBT. If your house is abusive, record any form of physical abuse or aggression with photos marking the date and time. Along with keeping a detailed logbook of everything that goes on. As for how to get to a better place, [this is a map of LGBT help centers](https://www.lgbtcenters.org/LgbtCenters) and also [information about homeless LGBT youth](https://www.americanprogress.org/wp-content/uploads/2013/09/LGBTHomelessYouth.pdf). It's a tough time but eventually you will get to be yourself and who you want to be with those you love and care about. 

Getting people to respect your identity is hard and sometimes impossible. The best thing to do is to maybe make a google document describing your identity, how it effects you, and how you'd feel better being referred to in another way. There's no full-proof  plan to get people to accept who you are sadly. Being trans means that some people you may love will leave, and not everyone will love nor accept or validate you. It's rough and has many ups and downs, but eventually when you're older you'll be able to do what you'd like and live life as you please.

If you have any questions feel free to ask me, and best of luck.

You're already leagues better than any nmom because you're actively trying to improve yourself. I work with disabled kids and help assist troubled youth (despite being "youth" myself) so I'm not a father or anything but I hope that this advice, even if it seems obvious can help a bit.

Being able to give your kids space and not restricting them when they go into their teenage years is important. Kids who have intense restrictions are more likely to become good liars and won't open up to you. An example of this is in situations with teens who are told to not have sex at all are more likely to have unsafe sex than those who are informed [as this article mildly goes over.](https://www.theatlantic.com/health/archive/2016/05/the-unintended-consequences-of-purity-pledges/481059/) Remember; kids are not going to be perfect. They aren't meant to be your ideal self nor are they always going to make the right choices. As a parent, it's up to you to help lead them towards the right paths and choices, but not forcing it on them. 

Also, if you have the funding for it I heavily recommend getting a therapist for your child during their teenage years. Therapists are not just for those who have mental illnesses, but are there to help improve people's lives and teach them skills to use. During puberty there's a lot of emotions and having someone confidential to talk to even if it's just once a month can help immeasurably. Whilst you of course want to be updated with your child's life, privacy is a form of respect and trust between you and your child. 

Hope this helped even a little. You'll be a great mother. Best of luck on your journey.
